planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall or early spring into consistently moist, humus-rich soil; established colonies spread readily by rhizome under a closed forest canopy.

directions: Pacific waterleaf is a rhizomatous woodland perennial native to moist lowland and low-montane forests from southern British Columbia through Washington and Oregon into northern California, where it forms loose colonies along shaded streambanks and beneath bigleaf maple and conifer canopy. Its slender, hairy petioles (the source of the epithet tenuipes) support deeply lobed, softly hairy leaves, and in mid-spring it sends up coiled, one-sided clusters of small bell-shaped flowers ranging from dull white to lavender-purple. Like its eastern relatives it prefers deep, humus-rich soil with reliable moisture and goes summer-dormant once forest soils dry out, so it pairs well with later-emerging ferns and other groundcovers that fill in as it fades. Indigenous peoples of the region historically ate the fleshy roots and young shoots, and the plant remains a useful, easy-care groundcover for the moist deciduous or mixed-conifer shade garden.
sources: Burke Herbarium Image Collection, University of Washington
